ancial proposals after they have been fully considered in the House, but I do not think there has been a single case where a government has been belaboured by its own followers into the reduction of a proposal, to its own humiliation, and has still said: We will retain office and accept the belabouring which our supporters have given us. That is the position of the minister to-day. Upon the original estimate the minister was on sound ground, as I said, but he is not on as sound ground today as he was two weeks ago.
I listened with the greatest interest and attention to the remarks of the hon. member for West Calgary, He has a very clear and convincing way of presenting a matter to this House. I listened with the greatest respect to what he had to say to-day, but I noticed at the end of his remarks he said: I am prepared to support this reduction, but I will not be satisfied with this item next year; I shall want a bigger reduction than $400,000 in this vote then.	[DOT]
Hear, hear.

"Hear, hear," resounds from a large portion of the Government benches. If it is the attitude of hon. gentlemen, that more should be cut from this vote next year, why not make a job of it to-day? There is no question as to what hon. members want who shouted "Hear, hear," just now. They want to cut annual drill to the vanishing point. In my humble judgment, Mr. Chairman, we have it practically to the vanishing point now, if we mean annual drill that is to be of any real service, and I know that is the opinion of the minister himself. You can cut down your vote for annual drill to a certain point, but there comes a point to go below which is a pure waste of money. Have we reached that point now?
I fear we have. The vote was for only $1,400,000 in the first place. It is now proposed to reduce it by $400,000, about thirty per cent of the whole. It could only have provided for partial training of a number of the units for a limited number of days in any event; it is now to be cut down by thirty per cent. It is a serious question whether the training that can be given on the balance will be of any practical advantage to the Dominion. My hon. friend from West Calgary has warned the minister that the vote must be cut still further next year, and his warning was heartily applauded by hon. members from the province of Quebec sitting opposite.
Why should my hon. friend always refer to the members from the province of Quebec? There are members from other provinces on this side of the House.
I referred to hon. members whom I saw applauding.
You have not very good eyesight.
I think it is fairly good. I made my remark in consequence of what I saw-
I am sick of that.
-whether my hon. friend is sick of it or not. I notice he was the minister selected to move this reduction of $400,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I tried to do it myself.

If the matter were to stop here, although the vote as it is proposed to reduce it is far too low, it might go through, but when warning is served from an important section of this House this this reduction is only a makeshift for the present year and that next year the vote must be still further reduced, it becomes a question whether you should not do it this year rather than waste the money in the interval. What I propose to do, and what I believe a considerable portion of this House is going to do, is to stand by the position which the minister took two weeks ago. He Was right then, and the Government knows he was right, and a majority of the members of this House know he was right, and I believe they will stand by him. This is a case where we are going to save the minister from himself, or, rather, I should have said, save him from his friends, and not permit him to be humiliated or "belaboured," or " big-sticked," or whatever you like to call it. When you know you are on solid ground, when you know the proposal is right, when you know the expenditure is warranted and cannot safely be reduced, when the Government has Committed itself upon the question, my judgment is that you should support the proposal made by the minister at first, and I certainly intend in my hubible way }to support it.
My hon. friend and colleague, the member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn), a member who has very much greater experience in military matters than almost any man in this House, in his speech this afternoon pointed out certain ways in which

Supply-Militia
money could be saved, not in actual training, but in administration, and it is possible there was a great deal in what he had to say. He based his argument upon this: Go ahead with your proposal as it stood two weeks ago; do not reduce it; persevere; go ahead; we will support you; you will find places in these estimates this year where, by reorganization and a change in administration, you can save large amounts of money, which you now propose to save 'by reducing the estimates before us by $700,000. In my humble judgment, and I speak only from what I have learned after two years in the department, it is far more important to pass this vote for annual training and annual drill than it is to maintain the Dominion arsenals at this particular moment. Looking over the estimates I find that the Government is practically closing up the Ontario arsenal this year, asking for only $25,000, which practically means only looking after the material and keeping the staff there; but $425,000 is being appropriated for the Quebec arsenal. Here is a suggestion for the minister:	Close the Quebec arsenal;
reduce the vote to $25,000, the same as for	the	Ontario	arsenal,	andthereby	save	$400,000. Then	you
would be able to have your annual training, which is a matter of the utmost consequence, and we would take a chance on the arsenal supplies for the future. I know the supply at Lindsay arsenal is away below the required reserve. Still, the minister does not hesitate to close that arsenal. I believe the arsenal at Quebec could be closed just as well, and $400,000 saved this year, provided1 the minister will apply that saving to the annual drill and training. Then the saving sought by the minister in moving to reduce this item for annual drill will be achieved, and if war does not take place 1 suppose no great injury will be done. We will have carried at least this point, that the men will receive the normal amount of training this present summer.

I had not intended
speaking on this question to-day, as I spoke when these estimates were up a week or so ago. I think I had better tell the committee at once that I am from Ontario, not from Quebec. I congratulate the minister upon his proposed reduction of these estimates, and I want to tell him that I believe ninety per cent of the people of Ontario will be pleased with his reduction. The people of Quebec are not alone in demanding that these estimates be reduced; I think the rank and file of, the people of the Dominion are looking for a reduction in the militia estimates. The military sentiment is still alive in this country. I well remember-and other members who were here last session or the session before will recall-that Mr. Mowat of Toronto, a supporter of the late government, introduced a resolution here asking practically for the compulsory military training of all young men in Canada bet-tween the ages of eighteen and twenty-five. They were all to be compelled to devote four weeks a year, for seven years, to military or physical training, the latter to all intents and purposes being the same as military drill. Now, military training did not raise the standard of morality in Europe, and it will not do so in Canada. A stream will rise no higher than its source, a nation is no stronger than its national homes; and one of the greatest assets in Canada to-day is the free and loyal patriotism to be found in every Canadian home. That was demonstrated during the war. A great deal has been said, and rightly said, in the way of compliment to the men of the militia who went overseas; but I want to assert that a great deal of commendation is due to those men who went overseas who never were in the militia at all. The long military training did not make the Germans more efficient on the battlefield. Our boys with their short military training proved themselves to be more than the equal of the Germans, and I am absolutely within the mark when I say this.
Now it has been insinuated that we who are in favour of this reduction of the estimates are not loyal people, that we want to do away with the militia. So far as I am concerned-and I think I can speak also for most of those who sit around me in this group-I assert that we are just as loyal as any other members in the House. But I have this to say further: We have more than the trained military men to be loyal to. We have a body of men who went overseas, did their bit in the trenches, came back home and went back to the farm and into other occupations. They require to be considered to-day. We must not forget also the women who sat up at night and worked just as loyally and faithfully in the interest of winning the war as the men who went overseas. These classes, whose interest I am afraid we are forgetting at the present
Supply-Militia

time, need to have their interests looked after just as much as the men who served in the militia.
It has been said that the arsenal at Lindsay has been closed. I am informed, and I think the statement is right, that no munitions were ever shipped from that institution although we have always voted money for it as long as I have been sitting here. I think therefore it is right to get rid of this building and not incur the expense of paying somebody to take care of it. I rose simply to endorse the action of. the minister and to tell him that he has my hearty support in reducing this estimate. I also believe he will have the support of the loyal people of Ontario and as well, perhaps, the support of the people of Quebec.

Did my hon. friend use
a big stick on the minister?

There must have been
a lot of big sticks left on that side when the Government moved over this way. I did not see any big sticks, and I did not use any-I am not that type of man.

I regret that in the discussion of this question-in which I have taken no part previously-there has been too much of a tendency, as there usually is when we differ from the government, to cry from the ministerial side "Tory, tory," and from the Progressive side-as my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Halbert) has just illustrated-to shout "Militarism, militarism." M'atters seem to have reached the stage in this House that if any hon. gentlemen sitting in this corner differ with either of the other parties they are denounced as a "Tory group" and in cases like the present as "a group of militarists."
And on this side from Quebec.
Well my hon. friend will not accuse me of ever saying anything against Quebec-
No, I admit that.
-but as a matter of fact my hon. friend will admit that on this occasion it was the members from Quebec, sitting opposite, who opposed this vote.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon; members from all the provinces spoke.

I admit that, but it was the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. [Mr. Halbert. 1
Po-wer) who moved to cut down the vote and he was supported by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), the member for Laprairie, and various others; and to mention that the hon. members from Quebec are opposing this vote is not necessarily to be regarded as saying anything derogatory towards the people of Quebec.
Does my hon. friend object to calling the members sitting around him Tories?
Well, personally I object to being called a Tory-
Why do you remain there then?
Because, Mr. Chairman, I am not in a Tory party.
Oh, oh.

That is why I remain here. I do not wish to go off into history but there was a time, a hundred years ago, when there were Tories; there are very few members of this House who accuse themselves of being Tories to-day. And if there are a few who do so that is their privilege; I do not say that myself; I repeat, I am not a Tory. And I say further, as regards the hon. members sitting around me, I do not consider that very many, if any, of them are Tories.
Name them.

To get back to the question I was discussing, which was militarism and the item before the committee. Because some of us in this corner have taken the position that this vote should go through, we are accused of being militarists by my hon. friend who has just resumed his seat and of being Tories by my hon. friend from St. James and his colleagues. Well, we are in the same position as the Minister of Militia who brought in these estimates, and he as my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has said, made a very fine speech in defence of his estimates the other night. I can say very frankly that it is the best speech by long odds that I have heard him make in this House.
But when my hon. friend from St. James makes the statement that he is voicing the views of the whole of Canada I think he is making rather a large statement; and when my hon. friend from North Ontario states that he is speaking for ninety per cent of the people of this country I think he is making a statement at least eighty

per cent too large. He was elected to represent one constituency and probably has a perfect right to speak for himself and for the people of that constituency; but I doubt whether he has any right to speak for my constituents on a question such as this. Now I arm not a militarist and I never have been one. In many ways I agree with the people who do not wish to spend too much money on militarism in this country, and personally I have always taken that attitude. However, in looking up the estimates which are before the committee I find in reply to a question by my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Church) that the expenditures in 1912-13 reached practically the same amount as the estimates which the Minister of Militia brought in for this year. Therefore if you consider that the value of a dollar to-day is worth perhaps sixty per cent of what it was in 1912, the estimates of the Minister of Militia to-day are really about forty per cent less in total than the estimates of the Militia Department in 1912.
But is the financial condition of the country to-day the same as it was in 1912?

No, I will admit the financial position of the country to-day is not the same as it was in 1912-13. But I would like to ask my hon. friend if the peace conditions of the world to-day are the same as they were in 1912-13. I have recently read-and I am sure my hon. friend has read it also-the statement made by Mr. J. H. Thomas, the Labour leader in England whom we all know, in which he says tha't we are as much upon the verge of war to-day in Europe as we were in the early days of 1914.
Does he not say in that statement that if there were a war England should not participate?

Yes, he does, but a
labour leader, John Burns, resigned from the cabinet in England in 1914, on the ground that England should not participate in the war, but she did participate; and I venture to say that the hon. gentleman from St. James (Mr. Rinfret), who is a very intelligent member of this House, will agree with me when I say that, in a war to-day, carried on in any part of this world, no one knows who will or will not participate until the war is over. The world is so close together, the transportation systems of the world are so well developed, the several nationalities of the world are so
highly developed to-day and so closely associated, that no one can tell who is going to take part in any war, and certainly the position of the Mother Country, and of the ancestors of my hon. friend in France, the mother country of most of the members from Quebec-
Every one of them.

No, the Minister of
Trade and Commerce (Mr. Robb) would hardly say that. It is true that France has taken a militaristic attitude, and I am not criticizing her for so doing, because she suffered severely in this war. In this 'country we do not know what is going to happen, if a war occurs. I sincerely hope, as everybody in this House hopes, that we will not have a war in the near future in which Canada will have to take part, but, while I deny absolutely the cry of militarism as applied to any of the members in this corner of the Chamber-and I deny it as regards myself because I am opposed to militarism-yet I do not believe in being so much of a peace-lover that I turn the other cheek to everybody who chooses to assail me. In the world to-day we do not know when we may require men who are trained in military affairs. It has been mentioned by lion, members on both sides of the House that many good soldiers who went overseas and made good records, including my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), were not in the militia. That is true, but I desire to point out to hon. gentlemen opposite that the thing which saved Paris from German invasion in 1914, and the thing which saved the alnea ports about that time, was the fact that there was in England a certain standing army, and because there was in France a very large standing army of trained men. If England and France had taken the attitude which is being taken to-day by a large number of members of this House, that we should have practically no military training at all in this country-because that is the attitude most of them take, judging by their applause to the remarks of the hon. gentleman from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie)-if they had taken that attitude back in 1912 and 1913, and thereabouts, there would have been nothing In the world to prevent Germany capturing Paris and conquering the world. 1 do not agree with the peace at any price attitude which our friend the former President of the United States assumed, which was a very noble idea, but he was not supported in his own country at the next elec-
Supply-Militia

tion, and he was not able to live up to that ideal throughout the war, because the United States found ultimately they had to take part in the war to help save civilization against the Germans.
I rose to make a few remarks against the cry of Toryism and militarism by men who happen to differ with other hon. members in this House. I am not a militarist, and yet when the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) brought in his original estimates, we agreed with him, and I think he should have stood by them. I do not like to tell an old trained politician what he should do, but it seems to me, if I were a minister, and brought in my estimates and made a strong speech, as the hon. gentleman did, in favour of them, and then was turned down by my own party I should feel it my duty to resign.

He did not have to
resign.

No, he retired. There are trained men in the leadership of the militia of every country who come to the front when war calls them to the front to fight; and, while it is true that a large proportion of the men who went from Canada were untrained men, the men who led them, in the large proportion of cases, were in the militia of Canada previously. I say that, although I served in France, and was never in the militia of Canada. The men who led the Canadian army, from Sir Arthur Currie down, were men who had served in the militia of Canada and had taken part in these camps. And my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Ross), who made such an eloquent speech this afternoon, was one of them. I have no reason for quarreling witih the Minister of Militia for retiring from his position, but I think he took the proper position the other day, and I should have had a strong admiration for him if he had stood by his guns, instead of making a noble retreat as one of my hon. friends on the other side termed it.
The antediluvian party.

I will refer to a few of the remarks made by the hon. ex-minister [DOT] of militia (Mr. Guthrie). It seems to me, in watching the debates in this House, that when the question of the militia estimates comes up, the real solid support for the retention of the maximum vote that can be put through this House comes from the party down in the corner. The hon. ex-minister of militia last year, and the year before, made positive assertion that the minimum amount of expenditure had been reached in the estimates that he had submitted to this House. To-day again he stresses the point that, if these material reductions have been made by the present Minister of Militia and Defence, we have now reached the danger point and dare not go lower. I have tried to make myself give credit to the hon. ex-minister of militia, while he was Minister of Militia and Defence, in that he did and should know more of the circumstances attending the militia of Canada than I could possibly know, but when I see him, as an individual, waver, as is shown by the recital I have given the House, likewise my faith in him must waver. It seems to me we have to form our own conclusions, and, in doing so, to bear in mind that we are here to do the will and the bidding of the people who sent us here. It seems to me that the militarist, if there be such a thing in Canada today-and I do not wish to make a specific charge that there are such people, although evidence has been submitted as to their existence in Canada-the militarist, as such, has had his day. Surely in the last five or six years his appetite for militarism should be satiated, and at the present time the lovers of peace throughout the country should have a little to say. The peace-loving people of Canada have not had an opportunity of expressing their opinion; they have not had an opportunity of showing to Canada and to the rest of the world what peace can do in the world, and I honestly believe the time has arrived when

Supply-Militia
they, at least, should he heard in the councils of the nation, and an attempt be made to give effect to the wishes of those people back home who find the sinews of war, the money with which to keep the machine going.
We will all admit the need of militia from time to time. For the benefit of the newspapers of Canada which have repeatedly attacked and denounced hon. members of the Progressive group who, conscientiously and with honest intent, have asked for reductions in these estimates, we should explain to this House and to the press of the country that, during the last three years< not one sentiment has been expressed from this Progressive group that gives them cause to believe that we do not approve of militia. We have repeatedly stated throughout Canada that we do not believe in extravagant expenditures, and during the past three years that I have been in this House positive proof has, on many occasions, been given in this Chamber of instances in which moneys have not been dispensed equitably, justly or for the purpose of militia and defence. One of the great factors that remain in the minds of the people is that moneys that we are supposed to be voting for militia and defence are being used, not for militia and defence, but just to maintain an aristocracy in this country.
As the House seems to be in favour of the proposed reduction, it is unnecessary to place upon Hansard the figures which I have compiled; but I desire to refer to a statement made by the ex-Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) with regard to the course that the minister takes before he presents his estimates to the House. He said that the minister's advisers will come and tell him what amount of money is required; that his advisers are capable men. We admit that they are capable men; but again I ask this pertinent question: Have the advisers to the minister, not alone in the Department of Militia, but in every other department, had an eye single as well to the individual who finds the money, who has to pay these obligations, as to the ways of expending that money? Are they as scientific in the matter of finding the money as they are in the methods of expending it? That is a thought that should remain in the minds of all ministers of the Crown. The exminister stated that the minister will be advised by his officials; that then he will submit his estimates to the Governor General, and that he will come back to this
House with the figures. When the exminister was making that statement, the thought occurred to me that, right at the moment when the minister presented his estimates to this House, somebody should rise and speak on behalf of the people because, in no instance in the remarks made by the ex-Minister of Militia, did he mention the cause of the people back home who provide the money. I am speaking for the people, and I am prepared to support the sentiment, as expressed by the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Halbert) , that ninety per cent of the people of Canada disapprove the huge expenditures that have taken place in Canada in the Department of Militia and Defence.
I have compiled a list of figures which shows that the officers in certain districts are in the proportion of one officer for every 2.3 men. I have talked with officers right in the city of Ottawa; I have met them in this very Chamber, and I have been told by honourable and gallant members of this House that they are supporting this reduction in the estimates; likewise, by gallant men in the city of Ottawa and throughout Canada that they approve our request_for a reduction, as they say at once that the money is not being equitably expended; that it is being used to pay officers' salaries; that we are over-staffed and under-manned; that in these vast areas it will take three days to bring the men in and to give them their equipment so that they may undergo training, and it takes the same time to take them home again. Is that militia? No, it is not militia, and I can show where, in a certain district of Canada, the officers themselves received between $6,000 and $7,000 more in salaries and allowances than the total expenditure on men, equipment, travelling expenses and everything else. It is that to which the people of Canada object and not to the false interpretation that is placed on our attitude here that we object to militia.
When the sentiment is expressed that we object to militia, attached to that is the sentiment that we are unpatriotic. That is not the case; but we have been taught to know the value of 100 cents, and that is what we have come here to plead for. We want those who receive the money to understand the value of 100 cents to-day. That is what I am pleading for, and that is why I ask for equitable treatment and equitable expenditure, not to cultivate any spirit of antagonism to national defence or to create the impression that we want to
Supply-Militia

defeat any defence party in Canada. When we have, in any district, officers in the ratio of one officer to 2.3 men whom the officers are supposed to train, we are not getting what we are supposed to have appropriated this money for. I ask some hon. members if the same thing was true in other districts and I was given to understand that the same condition obtained. I have another little complaint to make. I wish to state that the militaristic spirit seems to actuate the minds of some of those who get into authority. They have the conception that military law over-rides civil law, and it is the spirit of the Hun that prompts them to think and to speak in these terms and in this manner. It is only a matter of about two weeks ago that we had such an occurrence in Ontario. Liquor was supposed to be seized in a canteen and one of the excuses offered was that military law over-rides civil law. Let us come down to plain facts and be men, side by side, and I am sure the people of Canada will approve whatever we do in equity.
In conclusion, I wish to refer to some matters in connection with Military District No. 12, in which we have a certain condition that apparently does not obtain in any other military district in Canada.

Regina. I notice, in the
Auditor General's report, an item in connection with Military District No. 12, which, in my humble opinion, indicates that those who participate in these things seem to have very little regard for the people generally. I see an item here called "staff rides", and it is only in Military District No. 12 that this seems to be provided for. I notice that they have rented a hall at $5, and that they charge the Government up with $32 worth of theatre tickets. That is another conception of mind of the militarist, and I cannot understand why these people in that young military district should conceive the idea that they have a right to charge this country up with theatre tickets, while they are racing around the country. If one considers the amount of money that is set opposite each individual name, surely they can afford to purchase their theatre tickets. And the poor individual who has provided a hall receives a paltry $5 for his investment. As I think it is in the interests of a proper consideration of the estimates. I shall read these items

in order to place them on Hansard. They are:
Staff Rides: Prince Albert, Sept. 10, auto hire, $90, hotel expenses, $4.50; Saskatoon, Sept. 22-23, auto hire, $29 ; hotel expenses, $85.10 ; theatre tickets, $32; Regina, Sept. 29-30, auto hire, $119.50 ; hotel expenses, $79.15 ; rent of hall $5; North Battleford, Oct. 13-14, auto hire, $34.60; hotel expenses $27.75 ; Estevan, Oct. 26, hotel expenses, $13.40; auto hire, $3.50.
And by the way, $17 or $18 is the only money that has been spent in Assinihoia, although we furnished the money and in all ways taxed them. That is all the return we have for the huge amount of money taken from us in the way of appropriation. To proceed:
Moosomin, Oct'. 28, hotel expenses, $20, auto hire, $42 ; blue prints, etc., for rides, $24.69.
These are items which, I think, cannot be justified at all, and as I pointed out before, it appears that we have generals and staffs going around the country with presumption enough to charge these things against the country, when, from the sums of money placed opposite their names, we have at least the right to think they have been lavishly provided with funds of the people. House again in committee on Bill No. 6, respecting the Esquimalt & Nanaimo Railway Company.- (Mr. Tolmie)-Mr. Gordon in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: An amendment has been moved by Mr. Neill, that clause 1 of the said bill be amended by striking out all the words after the word "railway" in line 17 thereof. Shall the amendment carry?

I may remind the committee that the explanation of this amendment is that it brings this bill under the operation of the Railway Act of Canada. That is the whole sum and substance of it. An hon. member said the other night it was hardly necessary to do this because the company was on a different footing from that of any other company. But that is not so; this company is to be treated by this legislature, I hope, as any other railway

Esquimalt-Nanaimo Railway
company would be treated, and I have a precedent for that. In 1914 this charter was renewed for, I think, the fourth time; this is the seventh time renewal has been sought. But in the act of 1914 this sentence occurs:
-and shall within the two years expend thereof an amount equal to fifteen per cent of the capital stock.
That is precisely the clause that will operate under the Railway Act if my amendment passes; so that we have actually a precedent, not only as regards other railways, but as regards this railway, for the insertion of such a clause. All I am asking is that now, eight years after that was put in, the clause be once more inserted.

I come from the country affected by this railway. I have my good neighbour from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) on the north and the member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) on the south, and naturally I wish to remain on good terms with both. However, as we look down towards the south, following the laws of gravity, I naturally incline towards the hon. member for Victoria City on this subject. I know the country very well indeed through which this railway goes. Now, my good friend from Comox-Alberni has a faculty for painting word pictures which appeal to people-pictures to suit his own imagination, to a great extent. In this instance he is painting what to me is a cubist picture which I cannot understand. He has told the House at length that even if this bill is passed the Canadian Pacific will not build this line-even if they have one year or two years within which to commence. I quite agree that such may be the case. My hon. friend has told us of immense water-powers.

I rise to a point of order. The hon. member is out of order. We are not discussing the length of time, or the building or the not building; we are discussing an amendment which provides that the company shall spend fifteen per cent of the cost of construction within the time authorized.
If I am out of order, Mr. Chairman, I will bow to your decision. I have not taken up much time with respect to this matter. I am dealing with the principle of the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is discussing the first clause of the bill. In my opinion he is in order.

As I say, I know this country, and to show you that my hon. friend is painting a cubist picture I would point out that he said the other night that this question had a bearing upon the immigration problem of Canada. The district through which this road will eventually go is a small valley and we have plenty of people in our country to occupy that valley should we desire to do so. The valley has been logged over and agricultural possibilities are not quite as we would wish them, but there will be settlement in that district. To-day it would not pay the Canadian Pacific to build a road in there; it would not pay any company to do it. If that were not the case I would quite understand the reasonableness of bringing some pressure to bear on the Canadian Pacific to build the line.
Now, although we on this side have little reason for having any great affection for the Canadian Pacific, I do think that when it can be shown that the building of this road will be a profitable undertaking the Canadian Pacific will extend a line into that country.
The member for Comox-Alberni has said that there are radium mines in there. We all know what radium is; there are about eight ounces of it in the world, so that it would not furnish much tonnage. I have made some investigations on an island known as Valley island looking for other minerals, and I know it is claimed by prospectors to contain rock which shows radioactivity, which means that there is some radium in it. The member for Comox-Alberni told us the other night that this was the only radium mine in America. I may say that Gilpin County, Colorado, has contributed very materially towards the radium product of the world to-day, the ore being in the form of pitchblende or carnotite which furnishes the radium. The radium field, if there is one there, would not be affected in any way by this railroad. There is a first class road on Vancouver island which is traversed by hundreds in automobiles, a method of travelling much more pleasant than by train. This highway goes to a point just south of the mouth of the Campbell river, and this railway would pretty well parallel it. At present there is no great demand for a railway there to take timber from that country; the road so nearly conforms to the contour of the coast line that the timber naturally goes down into the salt water. Duncan's bay, to which this road is going to run, is just at the end of this magnificent automobile road on Vancouver island.

Esquimalt-Nanaimo Railivay
There are some settlers, very good men, engaged on little farms, 'but we all know that it takes more than a few scattered settlers to justify the building of a railway. 'If any other railway company in Canada was prepared to build in that territory, or if the road could be hastened in any way, I would not 'be on my feet to-night, but such is not the case. There are immense water-powers there. It is estimated in official reports that 200,000 horse power could be developed. There is also in that country a large iron deposit, which I have visited. It is a very promising deposit, but it requires considerably more work to demonstrate whether it is commercially valuable or not. When they start to develop these water-powers and this large iron deposit, we may expect this road to be extended, but at present, as an hon. gentleman said earlier in the session, it seems to me that the hon. member for Comox-Albemi is making "much ado about nothing."

The amendment which is proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) will, as he has stated, have the effect of bringing this railway under the Railway Act, clause 161. Now the intention of that particular clause was to prevent charter-mongering by irresponsible railway companies. I think that neither the Canadian Pacific nor the Canadian National roads can be included in that category, and therefore these restrictions are not necessary under the circumstances.
In the act passed in 1919, I think, incorporating the Canadian National Railways, a provision was inserted extending the charter powers of a number of railways included in that. system, Which had been previously authorized both by the federal government and provincial legislatures. In this connection certain privileges were granted to these roads. The provision in the act was as follows:
The times for the commencement and completion of the construction of the lines of railway specified in the second schedule to this act, which certain of the companies comprised in the Canadian Northern system were authorized to construct, are hereby extended for two years and five years after the passing of this act.
In the following year the Canadian Pacific Railway introduced a number of bills covering new branches and extensions of its lines, and the question was raised in the Railway Committee as to whether clause 161 of the Railway Act should be applied to these roads. It was pointed out to the committee, however, that the Canadian Pacific was entitled to the same treatment in this matter as the Canadian National Rail-
ways had received the year before. The committee agreed with this view and granted the request of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Strange to say, included amongst these bills was one relating to this very line of railway under discussion to-night. There was no difficulty over the acts passed in reference to the Canadian Pacific in the following year, 1921. The same privilege's were extended. In this particular case I can see no reason why an exception should be made, particularly as this bill has been submitted to the Railway Committee and has been accepted by them.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni the other evening referred to the Canadian Pacific securing an extension of their charter, and thereby possibly preventing other railways from constructing in that territory. I think that can hardly be the case because from 1916 down to 1920 the Canadian Pacific allowed their charter for this particular road to lapse and not a single railway company applied' to build (that piece of railway. In fact, located as it is, it is simply an extension of the Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway, and with no other railway on that end of Vancouver island no other company would build in that territory because they would have no road to link up with.
When the extension was applied for before the Railway Committee in 1920, Mr. McLeod, who is connected with the Canadian National Railways, was in attendance in connection with some Canadian National business, and he was asked by the committee if he had any desire to 'build a line of railway on the route laid out by the Canadian Pacific to Duncan's bay, and he informed the committee that he had no desire to build any railway or extend the Canadian National railway system to that section of British Columbia.
It has also been stated that it would be a great hardship to settlers if this railway was not built. As I have pointed out on a previous occasion, this railway runs almost parallel to the east coast of Vancouver island, and is located at no great distance from that coast, which is well supplied with a good steamer service. Moreover, the roads in that section, and in fact all over Vancouver island, are a very high class, so the farmer will suffer very little interference by deferring the construction of this railway.
I have pointed out already that to have the time for commencement and completion cut down to one year and three years, instead of two years and five years res-

Esquimalt-Nanaimo Railway
pectively, would be out of harmony with the rule adopted for the Canadian National Railways. As you are aware, Mr. Chairman, it will require a good deal of time to make arrangements to get the road under way, and if only one year was granted within which to commence construction, practically the whole of that year would be taken up in getting ready, and the railway company would probably have to apply for an extension of their charter inside of twelve months.
Under the present uncertain financial conditions, new railways can only be built after a very careful survey of the situation has been made, and there is reason to expect good results from the money expended. It is the hope and desire of this company to extend this road just as soon as their financial experts think there is a possibility of getting a reasonable return. Surveys have been already made and plans prepared.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni referred the other evening to the building of logging roads in that section of British Columbia. That was hardly a fair .comparison, because it is well known that these logging railways are not built in such a way that they would be accepted by the Railway Commission for either passenger or freight service.
In connection with the failure to renew bonding privileges, I may say that the committee's attention was called to the fact by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that this course was adopted for the reason that the railway company had no intention of building the road. In the 1920 act, this privilege was secured to the company, and therefore it is unnecessary to renew bonding privileges. It is quite true that the Canadian Pacific Bill No. 5, which is also before the committee at the present time, does make provision for bonding powers, but I am informed that the reason for that is that for one of these lines the charter has lapsed, and it became necessary on that ground to renew the bonding privilege. Railway construction costs at the present time are about fifty per cent higher than in 1913. Many of the materials entering into railway construction are about double in price or a little higher; rails are double what they were in 1913, ties are thirty to forty per cent higher. Taking materials generally, they cost much more than in 1913, and most likely very much higher than they will in a short time. I think that under these conditions, taking into consideration the fact that this is the largest railway corporation in the world and one that has done a great deal for the development of this country, it is only fair to grant to that company the same privilege that has been granted to other railways in Canada and trust in the bona fides of the company to build this road as soon as conditions justify them in doing so. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the bill should be allowed to pass the committee; I do not see that the objections raised to it are of a very serious nature.

The hon. member for
Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) was entirely out of order throughout his remarks and therefore I need not waste much time in dealing with them. The amendment before the committee is one relating to bringing this railway under the Railway Act, so that the company will have to spend fifteen per cent of the cost of construction. Has that anything whatever to do with the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo which dealt with the merits of the question of building or not building the railway? He drew attention to some of the remarks that I had made in that connection on a previous occasion and endeavoured to dissipate the effect of them. But I notice that in spite of all his attempts to do so he admitted the following facts: First, that there was a radium mine in the vicinity of the proposed railway; secondly, that there was water-power capable of producing 200,000 horse-power and, third, that there was a large iron deposit in the neighbourhood. Did I mention the iron deposit? No, I did not. But the hon. member has reminded me of it. So that the facts are that there is a water-power capable of producing 200,000 horse-power which can be easily harnesse'd; there is an iron deposit of the magnitude that he has indicated; and radium is present in the vicinity.
I think these are good enough reasons to require the completion of the railway; but as I do not want to be out of order, and as we are not dealing with these questions at the present time, I shall not refer further to the hon. member's remarks but go on and deal with the observations of the member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie). The latter dealt with the subject of the amendment in the early part of his remarks but wandered off the subject like my hon. friend from Nanaiimo later on. He said that the construction referred to in the Railway Act as regards the expenditure of fifteen per cent was not intended to
1606	COMMONS
Esquimalt-Nanaimo Railway
apply to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. If that is the case why was it not so stated in the Railway Act, and then there would have been no trouble at all? If it was not intended to make the Railway Act apply to one railway in particular, it should have been so stated in the act and then there would have been no confusion.
My hon. friend had to fall back on time honoured precedent and say that it had been done before. Well, one precedent is as good as another. I have quoted to you one precedent of the year 1914 when that identical clause was put into the Canadian Pacific Railway Bill. My hon. friend cited a case later on when it was not put in. We therefore have a choice between a precedent in one way, and another precedent in the other direction. But in view of the conflicting precedents let us go back again to the Railway Act of Canada which says this provision shall be observed. As regards the logging road he talked about, while I am out of order in referring to it I think I should he allowed the same latitude that was allowed my hon. friend. I have travelled over the logging road in question. It is forty miles long, is well ballasted, and the curves are good. The company who built it did not receive a subsidy of $6,000 a mile to construct it, nor did they hold the project back for twenty-two years by means of extensions of the charter.

House in committee on Bill No. 5, respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.-Mr. Knox.
On section 1-Extension of time for construction :
TMr. Neill. 1
I served notice of an amendment to this bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is moved in amendment by Mr. Carmichael to strike out in clause 1 all the words after the word "railway" in line 22, page 2, of the said bill.

It looks almost
futile to say anything in regard to this amendment, after the decision of the House on the amendment proposed to Bill No. 6, because this amendment is similar. It appears to me that this is a matter between a wealthy corporation and the supporters which it has, and the common people of Canada and the supporters which they have. I have no antagonism against the Canadian Pacific Railway, and it is not with any feeling of hostility that I move this amendment. I have every respect for that great corporation that, 37 years ago, commenced operations in Canada and to-day holds the position it does financially and as a service to the public. But, Mr. Chairman, when it comes to making a choice between a wealthy corporation and the common people of Canada, I am on the side of the common people of Canada.
I am particularly interested in subsections (c) and (d) of this clause, because the extensions proposed in those two subsections run through the constituency which I represent. Some time ago the Canadian Pacific Railway got a charter to build two extensions through this portion of the constituency. It may be in the minds of some hon. gentlemen that my constituency is in very bad shape, and has not any need of any railway extension, but'I wish to remind the House that the constituency is a very large one. It extends about 150 miles east and west, and between 75 and 80 miles north and south. While the southern portion of the constituency is hard hit financially, the northern portion is in good shape. The farmers are doing fairly well, the district is well settled, and the settlers have been in there for some 15 years. The land is productive, and has been producing for a number of years large quantities of grain. This district which is supposed _ to be served by these railway extensions is about 50 miles east and west, by about 35 miles north and south. You will readily understand that some of these settlers are from 20 to 25 miles from a railway point, and any person who has been raised on a farm can understand what that means in the

Canadian Pacific
hauling of grain. The large quantities of grain produced in this district have to be hauled a great distance, which goes a long way in reducing the profits which should go to the farmers. I have not proposed any amendment in regard to the time for building these extensions. This bill provides two years for commencing and five years for completing the work. I do not propose to make any change in the time. The amendment provides for the deletion of the words in the latter part of clause 1, which reads:
And if within the said periods respectively the said lines are not commenced, or are not completed, and put into operation, the powers of construction conferred upon the company by parliament shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said line as shall then remain uncompleted.
On a cursory examination it would appear that it did not make much difference whether these words 'were in the bill or out of it, hut, while I am not a lawyer, and never expect to be one, yet in my opinion the fact of these words being ip the bill makes a great difference in the operation of it, because when these words are in the bill, construction on these branch lines comes under the provision of this bill and is outside the provisions of the Railway Act of Canada, but when these words are eliminated from the bill, the construction of these branch lines comes under the provisions of the Railway Act of Canada. In section 3 of the Railway Act I find subsection (b), which reads:
*Where the provisions of this act and of any special act passed by the parliament of Canada relate to the same subject matter the provisions of the special act shall, in so far as is necessary to give effect to such special act, be taken to over-ride the provisions of this act.
That is exactly the provision which the Canadian Pacific Railway gets the advantage of if these words are included in this special act. The object of the amendment is to delete these words and bring the construction under the Railway Act of Canada.
Section 161 of the Railway Act reads:
If the construction of the railway is not commenced and fifteen per centum of the amount of the capital stock is not expended thereon in survey, purchase of right of way, and actual construction work, or, in the case of a branch or extension of the railway, if fifteen per centum of the bond issue authorized therefor is not expended thereon in actual construction work, within two years after the passing of the act authorizing the construction of such railway, branch, or extension, as the case may be, or, where the Parliament of Canada grants an extension of the time for commencing such
construction, within the time so granted; or, if the railway or branch, or extension, as the case may be, is not completed and put in operation within five years from the passing of such act, or, where the Parliament of Canada grants an extension of time for completion, within the time so granted; then the powers granted by suoh act or by this act shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the railway or branch or extension, as the case may be, as then remains uncompleted.
You will notice section 161 makes special provision for the expenditure of 15 per cent of the bond issue within the first two years, in order to enable the railway company to say they have commenced construction. That means something in Bill No. 5, because it is intended to build those two lines. The hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), in speaking to Bill No. 6, stated that it was not necessary to have restriction for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, because jthey did not_intend to Build the Tine" anyway, and he further stated that there was no provision for bonds in Bill No. 6. In Bill No. 5 provision is made for the issue of bonds or debentures to the extent of $40,000 per mile. If the construction of these branch lines is brought under the Railway Act of Canada, the railway company is compelled to expend 15 per cent of their $40,000 per mile within the first two years, in order to show that they intend to build these lines. That is just a mere matter of $6,000 per mile to be expended within the first two years, to show their good faith. Otherwise, if this provision of the Railway Act is not adhered to, the railway company might send a man out with a spade and throw up a little mound of earth within the first two years, and they would be clear, under the provisions of their own bill. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I submit that this amendment is a very vital one and deeply concerns the people whom I represent.
With regard to a company which is able to make such immense earnings, as the Canadian Pacific Railway has done in spite of hard times, financial distress amongst the farmers and business depression amongst our companies, a company that is able to pile up the large profits that the Canadian Pacific has done, that has been able in the past year to declare a 10 per cent dividend, and the hulk of whose stock is held outside Canada, so that the large proportion of its earnings is going outside of Canada, it seems to me it is not unrea

sonable to ask that such a corporation shall expend at least some of that money amongst the people who have helped to
Canadian Pacific

contribute towards those dividends which the Canadian Pacific has declared. Therefore, I have pleasure in moving this amendment.

I have pleasure in seconding the amendment; and while I am particularly interested in sub-clause (b), I should like to bring to the attention of the committee the wishes of the people of my part of the country for a railroad. This railroad was first proposed some years ago, and it should have been built, perhaps, before the war. The first survey through this part of the country was run by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and the bonds were at that time guaranteed by the Saskatchewan government. Through stress of the times, however, the charter was allowed to lapse until about two years ago when the Canadian Pacific obtained a charter for this road. No work has ever been done on it; and although people went into that part of the country from twelve to thirteen years ago with the expectation that the railroad would be built immediately, they are in dire need now for transportation facilities in order to market their produce.
This is not at all a line to be built with the prospect of the country being settled in the near or distant future; the country is settled all the way through from one end to the other. I know for a fact that, as regards some of the townships in that district, three-quarters of them are under cultivation, and the farms are as well established as in any other part of the country. The settlers who went in there first were mostly Ontario men and women, and besides raising grain, they have now herds of cattle. The position of the settlers in this district, although they are not as far from a railway as some people throughout the West are to-day, is a very difficult one. To the south of them it is impossible to reach the present Canadian Pacific line, the Pheasant hills branch, owing to the crossing of the Eagle hills. They are compelled to go north to the main line of the Canadian National Railways in order to market their crops. To do this they have to cross the river, and this is where the great problem comes in. When I was crossing there myself two years ago with a light rig, we first of all got on to one of the ferries which took us out into the middle of the bed of the river, and there we landed on a sand bank. After shifting up and down on that sand bank and getting into line with the cables, we got upon another ferry which landed us further out on an-

other sand bank, from which we had to make the best of our way to the shore. That day I met men with teams drawing about thirty bushels of wheat, and I wondered why they did not load their wagons. But the fact of the matter was that, if they could keep going over the bed of the river on these sand banks, they might get through; but if they once got down there was nothing for them to do but to unload. In the winter time it is impossible to go south owing to the Eagle hills which extend over a great deal of that country. Then to go north, several of them have to go together and put all the teams possible on to one load in order to get up out of the river bed. The shifting sand bars in the river, in the summer time or in the early fall, make ferry service very difficult, and sometimes these people have been even a whole month at a time without getting their mail from the post offices.
The marketing of their produce is the great handicap. When I went through there during the campaign of last fall, I found that most of these people were living in log houses; they were all postponing the building of better houses until the railway was in sight. They informed me that if the railway were at all in sight during the next year or so, they would settle down and make permanent homes; otherwise they would go back to where they came from and abandon the country. This is a well-settled district which is calculated to pay dividends on any railway that may be built at any time, and the Canadian Pacific is quite able at the present time to build this line. The Canadian Pacific has had for some years now a short spur out from Asquith to what is known as the gravel pit. If another twenty-five miles were constructed from the end of that line, such a railway would serve that country, and perhaps, it would relieve those settlers of many of the difficulties they are now under. The country is settled all the way through from Saskatoon to Cloan, and I think this Parliament should give these settlers, isolated as they are, the greatest consideration.

I wish to speak for a few minutes in support of the amendment. This suggested railway runs through a part of my constituency, and the people living along the route that the rails will follow have sent quantities of letters to me asking me to work against any further postponement of the building of this railway. Hundreds of these people are hauling their grain from twenty to twenty-five

Canadian Pacific
miles, and no one who has not hauled produce for twenty to twenty-five miles over a rough trail can have any appreciation of what sort of a task that is. It means not only a great waste of time in the summer when farmers should be spending all the time they have on field work, but a great hardship, particularly so in the winter time when most of their grain is hauled. These people have been in that part of the country for a good many years; they went there on the promise of the railway being built, and if that promise had not been made, the country would not have been settled. It is because promises have been made that railways would be built in so many parts of western Canada that we have to-day settlers living such distances from present-day railways, and this is unfair to these people.
We have heard a great deal about the necessity for bringing a large number of immigrants into the country, but I for one think it would pay us more to emphasize the need of providing the means by which to keep the present settlers that we already have. Because of promises that have been made in the past and not fulfilled, because of assurances in years gone by that railways would be built in this place and the other, while no attempt was made to carry out these undertakings, we are now losing our population. It does not matter how many settlers we bring into the country, or where they come from, when they live fifteen, twenty, twenty-five and thirty miles from a railway, they will not remain on the land. If settlers come into the country with the idea of building homes and being successful within a short number of years, we cannot hope at all to keep them if we do not carry out the promises we make. It is well known that in Alberta, where they do not get a crop every year, it requires on an average one crop in every three to pay for landing the produce at the seaboard. So that if you do not provide transportation facilities to farmers who are now living between twenty and thirty miles from a railway, you are only adding to the expense of growing grain; and besides that you are increasing the discontent of those who are already dissatisfied. No matter how much advertising you may do through Government agencies, so long as we have dissatisfied people at home who cannot make a success of their business because of the lack of transportation facilities, we cannot hope to secure new settlers, because those who are already 102
on the land here will do their level best to keep their friends, their relations and their acquaintances in different parts of the world from coming and settling in this country.
A questionnaire is in circulation in the neighbourhood through which this railway is supposed to be built, and in it questions are asked as to how many years ago a railway was promised, what was the amount of produce and stock raised in that part of the country, the number of miles people have to travel to get to the railway, and the cost per bushel for hauling produce that distance. And one rather interesting question is as to the number of. people who have left in the last ten years because the railway had not been built through this part of the country. I would call that last question particularly to the attention of hon. members, because it is one that should be seriously considered. If we are going to give the railway company the right to postpone indefinitely the building of this railway, then we are simply deferring the time when we shall be able to induce present settlers to stay on their farms. If we do not guarantee them transportation, and that within a reasonable time, we can expect to see settlers in the next ten years leaving in greater numbers than they have left in the past decade.

The amendment pending affects the extension of the charters of two roads in the constituency I have the honour to represent-charters that have been in existence for some time. A considerable portion of one of these roads has been constructed, and beyond the construction in both cases there are people who have long been in need of a railway for which they are still anxiously waiting. I have much sympathy with some things that have been said about the railway situation in Canada; but I am of those who are convinced that the railways in this country are worth to-day far more than they cost. These railways have served the country in time of great need and have vindicated themselves, and they are well worth a place in the history of the country. They did much during the Great War to carry to the front those things without which we could not have accomplished what we did; and I for one do not think that Canada has come to the time when we should quit and declare that we are bankrupt and shall go no further. I do not think it is time yet for us to say that we are "broke", and that we are going to lie down and wait for the sheriff.

This is going to be a great country, and the sooner we realize that and begin to get busy and start the wheels of industry the sooner we shall accomplish something. We need branch lines in order that we may feed and bring tonnage to the trunk lines that we have constructed. When we get those branch lines we shall increase business and population as well, and take care of those immigrants whom we
9 p.m. say we ought to secure. Now here is a proposition to extend certain charters. Under the terms of the proposal that is presented to us we say we will extend them for five years if these people throw a shovelful or two of dirt on each road within two years. I hope hon. gentlemen will see the reasonableness of that proposition. The railways should mean something when they ask for an extension for five years; otherwise-
